- When sentiment is strongly bullish (≥0.75) and model shows gradual upward trend, overestimate early peaks; correct by reducing slope after 3–5 consecutive bullish sentiment days.
- If official supply net is negative and sentiment is bearish, model tends to underreact — adjust forecast downward by 5–10% of recent 7-day mean if bearish sentiment persists.
- After sharp price spikes (e.g., >10% from prior 5-day avg), model often overshoots — cap forecast at +15% above peak for next 3–5 days unless sentiment confirms continuation.
- When official events are frequent (≥18/30d) and supply net is negative, model underestimates volatility — add 2–3% volatility buffer to forecast range if sentiment is neutral or mixed.
- If sentiment history shows alternating bullish/bearish cycles (e.g., 0.67, 1.00, 0.00), model tends to smooth transitions — force a 1–2 day lagged reversion to mean if price deviates >10% from 14-day moving average.
- For long-term (30d) forecasts, if sentiment is consistently bearish and supply net is negative, apply mean reversion bias: subtract 1.5–2.5% of 30d mean from forecast if price is above 1.5σ above mean.
